title: The Silk Road
summary: How a long web of trade routes linked China with Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe for more than a thousand years, carrying silk, other goods, and new ideas.
poll: Sharing ideas between lands is more important than trading goods.

versions.title: The Silk Road
versions.text:
Long ago, there were no planes. There were no trucks. But goods still went far. How?

They went on the Silk Road. It was not one road. It was a web of paths. The paths ran from China to the west. They went up big hills. They went on hot sand. They were more than six thousand kilometers long!

People used them to trade. To trade is to swap. You give one thing. You get a thing you want.

China made silk. Silk is a soft, shiny cloth. It is made by a small worm. China kept this a secret. In the west, lots of people wanted silk. So it cost a lot.

Men took goods on camels. A camel can walk far. It does not need much to drink. Big groups went on the trip. They stopped at inns to rest.

Few men went the whole way. They sold the goods to the next man. Then he took them on.

Not just goods moved. Ideas did too. China knew how to make paper. That idea went west.

Arab men sold goods on the paths too. They used land and ships.

The Silk Road was used for a thousand years.

versions.title: The Silk Road

Long ago, there were no planes or trucks. But goods still went from one side of the world to the other. How?

They used the Silk Road. It was not one road. It was a web of paths. The paths ran from China all the way west to the lands by the sea. They went over tall hills and across hot sand. In all, they were more than six thousand kilometers long.

People used the paths to trade. To trade is to swap one thing for a thing you want.

China made silk. Silk is a soft, shiny cloth. It is made from the threads of a small worm. China kept this a secret for a long time. Lots of people in the west wanted silk, so it cost a lot.

Men took goods on camels. A camel can walk a long way with not much to drink. Big groups of camels made the trip. They stopped at inns on the way to rest.

Few men went the whole way. Most sold their goods to the next trader. He took them on.

Goods were not the only things that moved. Ideas moved too. The way to make paper went west from China.

Arab traders sold goods on these paths too. They moved goods by land and by ship.

People used the Silk Road for more than a thousand years.

versions.title: The Silk Road
versions.text:
Long before airplanes and trucks, goods still traveled very far. Much of this trade moved along the Silk Road. It linked China with Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.

The Silk Road was not a single road. It was a network of routes, which means many paths that were linked to one another. Together, they stretched more than 6,400 kilometers. The routes crossed high mountains and harsh deserts. The Silk Road began more than two thousand years ago, when China sent travelers west to make contact with other lands.

The routes were named after silk, a smooth, shiny cloth. Silk is made from threads spun by silkworms. For hundreds of years, China kept the way of making silk a secret. People in faraway lands paid high prices for it.

Merchants, or traders, carried many other goods too. Spices, paper, tea, and fine dishes went west. Glass, gold, and horses went east.

Merchants often traveled in a caravan, a large group of people and animals that make a trip together. Camels were ideal, because they can go for days without water. At night, caravans rested at inns along the road.

Few merchants traveled the whole route. Instead, goods were passed from trader to trader, like a relay race.

The Silk Road also helped people exchange ideas. For example, papermaking spread west from China and reached Baghdad by around the year 800.

Arab merchants were an important part of this trade. They carried goods across the Arabian Peninsula and on ships to busy ports.

The Silk Road was used for more than a thousand years, until sea routes became more popular.

versions.title: The Silk Road
versions.text:
Long before airplanes and trucks existed, goods still traveled across enormous distances, and much of this commerce moved along the Silk Road, which connected China with Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.

The Silk Road was not a single road but a network of routes, meaning many paths that connected to one another and together stretched more than 6,400 kilometers across towering mountains and harsh deserts. It began more than two thousand years ago, when China's Han dynasty sent an official named Zhang Qian west to establish contact with distant kingdoms. The name "Silk Road" itself is much newer, since a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen, popularized it in 1877.

The routes were named after silk, a smooth, shiny fabric produced from threads spun by silkworms. Because China kept the method of producing silk a closely guarded secret for centuries, people in faraway lands paid extremely high prices for it.

Merchants carried many other goods as well, so that spices, paper, tea, and fine porcelain traveled west, while glass, gold, and horses traveled east.

Merchants often traveled in a caravan, a large group of people and animals journeying together for safety. Camels were ideal for this purpose, because they can survive for days without water. At night, caravans rested at caravanserais, roadside inns that were often built about a day's journey apart.

Few merchants traveled the entire route. Instead, goods were passed from trader to trader, almost like a relay race, and their prices rose at every stop.

The Silk Road also allowed people to exchange ideas. For example, the knowledge of papermaking spread west from China and reached Baghdad by approximately the year 800, which helped books become more common.

Some travelers left famous records of their journeys. Marco Polo, a merchant from the Italian city of Venice, traveled to China in the late 1200s, and the book about his adventures made many Europeans curious about Asia.

Arab merchants played an important role in this trade, transporting goods across the Arabian Peninsula and on ships through the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf to busy ports, and this sea trade is sometimes called the Maritime Silk Road.

The land routes were used for more than a thousand years, until sea routes gradually became more popular.

Why camels have humps
How the first planes carried goods
Paths used to trade goods and ideas

MID.prompt: The Silk Road carried both goods and ideas. Which do you think was more important? Use at least two details from the article to explain.
checklist: I gave a clear answer to the question.
I supported my answer with at least two details from the article.
I used words such as merchant, route, or exchange correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: I think ideas were more important than goods on the Silk Road. For example, papermaking spread west along the trade route from China and reached Baghdad by around the year 800, which helped people share and copy knowledge much more easily. Also, merchants traveling in a caravan exchanged more than silk and spices; they exchanged customs and information as they moved from one trader to the next. This network of exchange shaped history long after the goods themselves were used up.

questions.stem: According to the article, what were caravanserais?
options: Roadside inns about a day apart
Ships that sailed the Red Sea
Markets in the city of Venice
Factories that produced silk
questions.why: The article describes caravanserais as roadside inns that were often built about a day's journey apart.

wrong.B: Ships are part of the Maritime Silk Road, not caravanserais.
wrong.C: Venice is Marco Polo's home city.
wrong.D: The article does not mention silk factories.

questions.stem: Sea trade through the Red Sea and Arabian Gulf is called the "Maritime Silk Road." What does maritime mean?
options: Very old
Related to the sea
Related to the desert
Very expensive
questions.why: The term describes trade carried on ships by sea, so maritime means related to the sea.

wrong.C: The desert routes were the land routes.
wrong.D: Maritime is not about cost.

questions.stem: Why did the price of goods rise as they moved along the Silk Road?
options: China placed heavy taxes on every merchant who traded in Europe.
Camels demanded payment.
Goods became heavier over time.
Each trader along the way raised the price.
questions.why: The article explains that goods passed from trader to trader like a relay, and their prices increased at every stop.

wrong.A: The article does not mention Chinese taxes in Europe.
wrong.B: This is not a real reason.

questions.stem: Why might Marco Polo's book have been important to the history of the Silk Road?
options: It contained the secret of making silk.
It ended almost all of the trade between Europe and Asia for centuries.
It made Europeans curious about Asia.
It named the Silk Road.
questions.why: The article says his book made many Europeans curious about Asia, which could encourage more interest and travel.

wrong.A: The article does not say his book revealed silk-making.
wrong.B: The article gives no sign that it ended trade.
wrong.D: The name came from von Richthofen in 1877.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why did the overland routes become less important?
options: Sea routes became more popular.
Camels disappeared from Asia.
China stopped making silk.
Papermaking was forgotten.
questions.why: The article ends by saying the land routes lasted until sea routes gradually became more popular.

wrong.B: The article does not say camels disappeared.
wrong.C: There is no evidence China stopped making silk.
wrong.D: Papermaking spread; it was not forgotten.

questions.stem: How does the paragraph about papermaking support the author's larger point?
options: It shows that Baghdad was the final stop at the far western end of the Silk Road.
It proves that silk was cheaper than paper.
It shows that ideas spread and changed daily life.
It explains why caravans traveled at night.
questions.why: Papermaking reaching Baghdad and helping books become common shows that ideas traveled the routes and had lasting effects.

wrong.A: The routes continued far beyond Baghdad to Europe.
wrong.B: The article does not compare these prices.
wrong.D: The paragraph is not about caravans.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say the most valuable thing carried on the Silk Road was not silk but ideas. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that ideas were the most valuable thing carried on the Silk Road. One piece of evidence is that papermaking traveled along this network from China and reached Baghdad around the year 800, spreading a technology that changed how people recorded and shared commerce and knowledge across continents. Another piece of evidence is that Arab merchants carried goods across the Arabian Peninsula and onto maritime routes, connecting cultures over both land and sea for more than a thousand years. While silk was valuable in its own time, the spread of ideas through this network kept shaping the world long after the Silk Road's caravans stopped traveling.
